analysis.one_liner: Bans data brokers from selling people's health and location data.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban data brokers from selling Americans' health and location data never received a hearing or vote, dying in a House subcommittee at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for data brokers — companies that gather or buy information about people and sell it — to sell, license, trade, or share anyone's health data or location data. "Health data" is defined broadly: it covers seeking or receiving health services, pregnancies and miscarriages, disabilities, and mental or physical health conditions; "location data" can pinpoint where a person or their phone has been, past or present. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could sue to stop sales and delete wrongly sold data, individuals could sue too, and penalties could reach 15 percent of a parent company's yearly revenue. The FTC would get $1 billion to enforce the ban.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be ordinary people: anyone whose phone constantly logs their movements, and anyone whose health information — appointments, prescriptions, pregnancies, diagnoses — is currently gathered, inferred, and sold. The FTC would gain new authority and a $1 billion fund to enforce it. People whose data had already been sold could seek its deletion and damages in court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone with a phone and health records

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for data brokers to sell, resell, license, trade, transfer, or share a person's health data or location data, whether that data was directly given or inferred.
Defines health data broadly: it covers seeking or receiving health services and any physical or mental health condition, expressly including pregnancy and miscarriage.
Defines location data as anything capable of determining a person's or a device's past or present physical location.

Gives the FTC, state attorneys general, and private individuals the power to sue, win deletion of wrongly sold data, and collect damages; civil penalties can reach 15 percent of the ultimate parent entity's prior-year revenue.
Appropriates $1 billion to the FTC to carry out the enforcement work.
Preserves legitimate channels: HIPAA-compliant handling of health information, newsworthy publication, and disclosures the individual authorizes remain allowed.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the app-and-advertising companies that monetize location and health data would lose their core product and face penalties up to 15 percent of parent-company revenue. Taxpayers would fund the $1 billion FTC appropriation. Legitimate uses — HIPAA-compliant care, journalism, and authorized sharing — are carved out, so the cost falls mainly on the commercial data trade.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and mobile ad companies

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates $1 billion in new taxpayer money to the FTC, available through 2032, on top of the agency's existing budget — a substantial public cost for enforcement.

The protection is not total: anything permissible under HIPAA privacy rules stays legal, so hospitals, insurers, and their business associates can keep handling health information as they do today; the bill closes the broker market, not the medical-system data flows.

Enforcement is concentrated in Washington: FTC actions go only to the D.C. federal district court and every appeal goes only to the D.C. Circuit, which could slow cases and keep litigation far from the people affected.

The ban reaches data that is merely 'inferred,' and the FTC would have to define key terms by rule within 180 days of enactment — a short deadline that risked contested rules, and the law's real-world effect would depend heavily on how those rules were written.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the gain would have been large: their most sensitive data — where they go, whether they are pregnant, what conditions they have — would have stopped being a commodity, with deletion, damages, and penalties to back it up [S3]. The costs are real but narrower: $1 billion in federal money for enforcement [S3], a compliance shock to the data economy, and design compromises an honest supporter should acknowledge — HIPAA-covered data flows continue untouched [S3], all federal cases and appeals are funneled into Washington, D.C. courts [S3], and a 180-day rulemaking deadline risked rushed rules. On balance, the public benefit outweighs the fiscal and design costs.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the last three months of the session, the bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then its consumer protection subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon (D-PA) introduced the Health and Location Data Protection Act of 2022 on October 7, 2022, with seven Democratic cosponsors.
The House referred the bill to the Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and to the committee's Consumer Protection and Commerce Subcommittee three days later.
No hearing, markup, or vote ever followed; the bill received no further action and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Had it passed, the bill would have made it unlawful for data brokers to sell, resell, license, trade, transfer, or share health data or location data, whether declared or inferred.

The bill provided for enforcement by the FTC, state attorneys general, and private suits, with civil penalties up to 15 percent of the ultimate parent entity's prior-year revenue, plus a $1 billion appropriation for the FTC.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers and the advertising ecosystem that buys and resells health and location data are better off: the market the bill would have shut down continues, and no comparable ban was enacted. The public gains nothing from this outcome.

sides.party_line_note: All eight recorded supporters — the sponsor and seven cosponsors — were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and no vote was ever taken to test the broader split.

industries.note: The bill's direct target: companies that collect, buy, or infer data and then sell it would be barred from selling or sharing anyone's health or location data, and wrongly sold data could be deleted, with penalties up to 15 percent of parent-company revenue.
Phones constantly report location, and adtech firms that buy and resell it to target ads fit the bill's definition of a data broker; the ban would cut off that revenue stream.

industries.industry: Health apps, pharmacies, and telehealth companies that sell user data
industries.note: Their sales of users' health-related data outside the HIPAA system would be banned; HIPAA-compliant transfers stay legal, so companies inside that system keep operating much as before.

industries.industry: Hospitals, insurers, and their business associates (the HIPAA system)
industries.note: The bill carves out anything permissible under HIPAA privacy rules, so the existing hospital-and-insurer data-handling system keeps its rights while brokers outside it are shut out.
